Peekskill.wildlife_intro:
Peekskill is Westchester's Hudson river city — an older, denser, hillier place than the county's suburbs, with pre-war homes and apartment buildings climbing from the waterfront toward the wooded highlands behind it. Norway rats are a standing call in the oldest downtown and riverfront blocks, raccoons and squirrels fill the hillside attics, and bats roost in the eaves of the Victorian-era housing on the upper streets. The bay and creek at the city's foot concentrate night animals along the shore.

Peekskill's inspections run downhill in every sense: cellar and foundation entries near the water, porch and addition junctions on the slopes, tired rooflines up top. Our crew inspects Peekskill homes at all three levels, removes the animals, and seals accordingly — treating rat complaints at the foundation where they belong, and attic complaints at the roofline, instead of selling one fix for both.

faqs.q: Why do raccoons thrive in Rye?
faqs.a: Salt marsh, Sound shoreline, and sanctuary woodland give raccoons food and daytime cover, while the city's large older homes give them chimneys and attics a short walk away. Our crew removes them and caps and seals every entry, including the guest-structure voids that restart the cycle.

Rye.wildlife_intro:
Rye is Westchester's Sound-side enclave: a small city of large older homes, waterfront estates, and groomed streets between Long Island Sound and the Blind Brook corridor, with the Playland and nature-center shoreline at its south. Raccoons are the marquee call — big chimneys, big attics, and marsh-edge forage make the city ideal for them — followed by bats in the older homes and squirrels throughout the heavy canopy. The marshes and the Edith Read Sanctuary keep wildlife density high along the shore.

Large homes mean large inspections in Rye: long rooflines, multiple chimneys, guest and pool structures. Our crew inspects Rye properties as the compounds many of them are, removes the animals, and seals the main house first, then the secondary structures that keep restocking the grounds. Marsh-edge lots get ground-level screening attention too, because the same corridor that feeds raccoons gives skunks their dens.

faqs.a: Canopy density: the village's mature oaks overhang roofs on street after street, feeding a large gray squirrel population and giving it aerial access to soffits. Our crew identifies both the entries and the access limbs at inspection so the fix addresses the route, not just the current tenants.

Scarsdale.wildlife_intro:
Scarsdale is the archetypal Westchester village suburb — Tudor and colonial homes on groomed, heavily canopied lots, organized around its five neighborhood elementary districts. That canopy is the wildlife story: gray squirrels are relentless in Scarsdale attics because the oaks bridge to nearly every roof, raccoons den in the village's many masonry chimneys, and bats use the eaves of its substantial pre-war housing. The Bronx River corridor along the village's west adds skunks and ground-level movement.

Scarsdale's sealing standard has to be high because the pressure is: a single missed gable gap reopens a house within a season. Our crew inspects these homes junction by junction — dormers, additions, and the junctions Tudor rooflines multiply — removes the animals, and seals completely, then tells you plainly which overhanging limbs are functioning as squirrel bridges and should come back.
